"Didi, the new man at Kaka's house doesn't talk to anyone," Vijay said, peeling a groundnut. "He sits on the step and reads books all evening."
"So?" Sarita asked, not looking up from her homework.
"So he's a librarian. Obviously."
"Why obviously?"
"Quiet. Books. Glasses. That's a librarian."
"Vijay, how many libraries are there in our whole taluka?"
He thought. "One. Near the bus stand."
"And how many farms?"
"Hundreds. Everyone has a farm."
"So which is there more of, librarians or farmers?"
Vijay frowned at the groundnut shell. "Farmers... but he really looks like a librarian!"
"Farmers can like books too. Appa reads the newspaper twice every morning."
"Hmm. Maybe he's a farmer who reads," Vijay said slowly. "I'm still asking him tomorrow."

qa.q: What does the new man at Kaka's house do every evening?
qa.a: He sits on the step and reads books all evening.

qa.q: Why does it feel so obvious to Vijay that the man is a librarian?
qa.a: Vijay feels confident because the man is quiet, with books and glasses, matching Vijay's picture of a librarian so well that the match feels like proof. Vijay forgets there is one library but hundreds of farms.

qa.q: What question helped Vijay, and what could he ask himself next time?
qa.a: Sarita's question about how many libraries and farms made him count. Next time he could first ask how many people around him do each job, and only then look at the clues.

qa.q: How might the new man feel if Vijay told him, "You must be the librarian"?
qa.a: He might be amused or puzzled, especially if he is a farmer who simply enjoys reading in the evening.

grounding: It shows a child jumping from 'quiet and reads books' to 'librarian' while forgetting how many more farmers there are.

qa.a: He might find it funny, or feel a little misread, since loving books is part of his life as a farmer too. 🙂

Class 4B, Thursday. In our guessing game today I described a stranger: a quiet man who loves reading, always with a book in his bag. Vikas shouted "Librarian!" at once, and most hands went up with him. Deepak said "farmer", mostly as a joke. I asked Vikas how many librarians he knew. "One, at the town library." How many farmers? passage: Everyone at college still calls me Forward-Yamini, so here's why I stopped forwarding stuff. In Class 9, Vaibhav was absent for four days, and a girl from the next section told us he'd been expelled. Her mum works in the school office, she said, and she described everything: the principal slamming a blue file shut, Vaibhav's father walking out into the rain without his umbrella. I believed every word. I even messaged three people. Then on Friday Vaibhav walked in with a chess trophy. He'd been at a district tournament. Honestly, in ten years at that school I'd heard of maybe one expulsion, ever. But the blue file and the umbrella felt so real that I never counted. Now when a story has lots of juicy details, I ask how often that thing actually happens.

qa.a: He'd been at a district tournament, and he walked in with a chess trophy.

qa.q: Why did Yamini believe the expulsion story so completely?
qa.a: The blue file and the umbrella in the rain made it feel like an eyewitness account, so Yamini never stopped to count how rare expulsions were at that school.

qa.q: What habit did Yamini build, and why does it work?
qa.a: Yamini now asks how often a thing actually happens whenever a story is full of juicy details, which puts the plain odds back beside the vivid story.

qa.q: What was it like for Vaibhav to be the subject of this rumour?

passage: My younger sister Lakshmi stopped revising on Tuesday evening. I noticed because her chemistry notes stayed shut on the bed and she was humming. qa.a: Checking the board's own website together worked, because it tested the vivid message against a reliable source instead of arguing about the stamp.

qa.a: Sangeeta sees only the outside, the shut notes, the humming and the relief, and says she doesn't know what was in Lakshmi's head.

Counselling note, Wednesday.
Jomon (second year, B.Com) came in with his friend Avni, who waited by the door. He had a slip from Saturday's campus health camp: one screening result for a rare blood condition marked "positive, repeat test advised". He had read that the screen is "95% accurate" and was convinced that meant he almost certainly had it. He said he hadn't slept much, and he kept rereading the slip. I did not interpret the result; that is not my role. Instead we wrote down his questions for the doctor, including "How many people who test positive on this screen actually turn out to have it?" He booked the repeat test before leaving. Avni offered to go with him. I will check in on Friday.

qa.q: What did Jomon's slip from the health camp say?
qa.a: One screening result for a rare blood condition was marked "positive, repeat test advised".

qa.q: Why does "95% accurate" make Jomon feel almost certain he is ill?
qa.a: Jomon feels frightened because "95% accurate" sounds to him like a 95% chance he has the condition, and the slip in his hand feels more real than the fact that the condition is rare to begin with.

qa.q: How did the counsellor help without giving medical advice?
qa.a: The counsellor helped Jomon write questions for the doctor, including how many positives turn out to be real, and he booked the repeat test.

qa.q: What might this week be like for Avni?
qa.a: Avni is probably worried and trying to stay steady for a friend, which is why Avni came along and offered to go to the test. 🤍

passage:
Shift supervisor's note, Line 3, Tuesday.
At 9:10 the new vibration sensor flagged pump P-7 as "failure likely". Two operators wanted to shut the line straight away. Chandrika, our process engineer for eight months, asked everyone to wait five minutes. She pulled up the maintenance log first: across our forty pumps, real failures have been rare, a handful in three years, while this sensor has already sent eleven alerts since March. "So on its own, an alert is weak," she said. Then she checked what was specific to P-7: temperature normal, no odd noise, but a slight rise in vibration over two weeks. She called the supplier's engineer and asked what share of alerts had turned out real at other plants. We booked an inspection for the weekend instead of stopping production. I've asked her to show the team how she did this.
Amandeep

qa.q: How many alerts had the new sensor sent since March?
qa.a: Eleven alerts.

qa.q: Why did Chandrika want to check the maintenance log before reacting?
qa.a: She thought an alert only means something once you know how rarely pumps actually fail, and she didn't want to stop the line for what might be a false alarm.

qa.q: What steps did Chandrika follow, and why do they work?
qa.a: She started with how often failures really happen, then looked at P-7's own signs, then asked the supplier's engineer to explain the alerts. That weighs the alert against the odds instead of treating it as proof.

qa.q: How might the operators who wanted to shut the line see Chandrika's pause?
qa.a: At first they might think she was being slow or risky, but watching her check the log and P-7's readings could make the weekend inspection feel like a safe middle path.

grounding: It shows a careful engineer starting from how common pump failures are, adjusting for P-7's evidence and asking an expert to explain the alerts.

Friday night
Papa's health-check report came this morning. One line in red: a screening marker "raised", with a note about a rare liver condition. Papa went silent at breakfast and Mummy started calling relatives.
I made myself do what I learned in my stats elective. First question: how common is this condition in people Papa's age? I didn't know, so I wrote it down. Second: his other results were all normal, he isn't tired, he walks every evening. That pulls things down a bit. Third: the report says "suggest repeat test", not a diagnosis.
At the clinic I asked Dr. Ramesh straight: "Out of people who get this flag, how many actually have it?" He smiled. "Good question. Most don't. Let's repeat it and see."
Papa laughed for the first time today.
- Jatin

qa.a: A screening marker was "raised", with a note about a rare liver condition.

qa.q: What was Jatin worried about when writing the questions down?
qa.a: Jatin was worried the fear would run ahead of the facts, since Papa had gone silent and Mummy was calling relatives.

qa.q: Why was Jatin's question to Dr. Ramesh a good one?
qa.a: Asking how many people with the flag actually have the condition gets the doctor to explain the result in context, instead of the family guessing from one red line.

qa.a: Papa went from silent at breakfast to laughing, because the doctor's explanation made the flag feel less like a verdict.

The bus to Kharghar was so packed that Rukmini had to shout over the horns. "Aparna hardly talks, but her notebook is full of sketches. Faces, trees, even the canteen uncle."
Her cousin Nitin, squeezed against the door, yelled back a game. "Okay, which is more likely? One: Aparna is an artist. Two: Aparna is an artist, a shy one, and she secretly writes poems."
"Two! Obviously two," Rukmini said. "That's so her. I can totally see her writing poems at night."
Nitin grinned. "Every shy poet-artist is still an artist. So number two can't beat number one."
The bus braked hard and Rukmini grabbed the rail, frowning. "But two sounds more true."
"Sounds, yes," Nitin said. "You just added one more thing that has to be right."
Rukmini stayed quiet until her stop, still picturing Aparna's secret poems.

qa.a: She could ask whether one option is just the other one plus extra details; if it is, the shorter one is always at least as likely.

qa.a: She might be amused, or a bit uneasy that people built a whole story about her from her quietness and her sketches.

passage: People ask what I, Madhav, actually do in meetings. Mostly I listen. Last month Shankar pitched a plan to our team: a new delivery route for the bakery's orders. It was gorgeous. Step one, the new van arrives by the 5th. Step two, the two drivers finish training in a week. Step three, the café chain signs by the 15th. Step four, our order software syncs with their system. Everyone nodded, me too at first. Then I counted. Four steps, and every one had to land on time. I said, "Each of these is fairly likely on its own. All four together? A lot less." Shankar looked annoyed for a second, then laughed and said we'd plan a backup for the van. It wasn't about shooting him down. It was just counting.

qa.a: Tushar now sees it as helpful rather than spoiling the fun, which is why he admitted Omkar was right about the lunch.

In Vadipatti, the under-12 kabaddi team practised on the dry field behind the temple. Muthu had noticed something. Every match he played in his faded red shirt, the team won. The week it tore and he wore blue, they lost to the next village.
"It's the shirt," he told his sister Shalini, holding it up like a flag. "It brings the luck."
Shalini, sewing the tear by lamplight, looked up. "That week, wasn't Selvam down with fever? And Kavitha teacher had gone to her mother's village, so nobody made you practise."
Muthu frowned. "That's also true."
"So which one did it, the shirt or the missing people?"
He pulled the shirt on anyway. "Maybe both. I'm not taking the chance."

qa.a: He half sees her point, but the pattern of wins still feels real, and wearing the shirt feels safer than risking a loss.

qa.q: How could Kavitha teacher help the team think about the shirt?
qa.a: She could list with them what was different on the losing day, like Selvam being ill and no practice, so they see other reasons for winning and losing.

qa.q: What would change if Muthu kept wearing the red shirt but the team stopped practising?
qa.a: They might start losing even with the shirt on, which would show that the shirt was never what made them win.

grounding: It shows a village boy deciding his red shirt causes wins because the shirt and the wins appeared together.
